disease_info: Persistent Depressive Disorder (dysthymia) is characterized by a chronically low mood lasting at least two years in adults, with only brief periods of remission. Individuals often function day to day but at a reduced level, experiencing the depression as part of their usual personality or life, which can delay recognition and treatment. Compared with major depressive disorder, the symptoms are typically less acute but more enduring, leading to long-term interpersonal, occupational, and quality-of-life impairment. It frequently coexists with other psychiatric conditions and may be punctuated by superimposed major depressive episodes ("double depression").

narrative.stressor: Johnathan traces the beginning of his prolonged low stretch to the period surrounding his divorce a little over three years ago, when his long hours on municipal contracts and weekend side jobs had been straining the marriage for years. After the separation, he poured himself even more into work and community projects, taking every landscaping contract he could and volunteering at the community garden to avoid being alone in his small apartment. Over time, he noticed that activities that used to restore him—weekend hikes above Aguadilla, cooking elaborate family meals, leading bomba dances—felt more like obligations he was going through out of habit, and he started turning down invitations from relatives, including Sunday dinners with his parents. It was only when his sister commented that he seemed like he was "just existing" and his crew started pointing out his increasing rigidity with schedules and lack of interest in new designs that he agreed to see a doctor at a local clinic, who then referred him for a psychiatric evaluation.
narrative.chief_complaint: I’ve felt this low, empty mood hanging over me for years now, like I can’t shake feeling down no matter what I do.

narrative.stressor: For Loi, the depressive period gradually took shape after her company underwent a major restructuring a little over three years ago, increasing her claims load and shifting her from field work she enjoyed to more remote desk-based assessments. The longer hours, constant video calls, and pressure to mentor younger adjusters while learning new software left her feeling drained by the end of each day, and she began skipping her weekend hikes and painting sessions, telling herself it was just a busy season. As this "busy season" stretched into years, she noticed that even vacations to wine country and carefully planned trips abroad failed to restore her usual sense of engagement, and her husband pointed out that she no longer seemed to take pleasure in planning their outings or photographing the Temecula hills. When she started making small errors in reports and needing multiple days to complete tasks that once took an afternoon, she became worried about her performance reviews and, at the suggestion of a colleague who had sought help for burnout, she contacted her primary care physician, who recognized a longstanding mood issue and referred her to psychiatry.
narrative.chief_complaint: For the past few years I feel worn out all the time, like I’m running on empty even when I’m not doing that much.

narrative.stressor: Brad’s low-grade depression emerged insidiously in the years following his retirement from biomedical engineering, a transition he had initially approached with excitement about having more time for art, music, and mentoring. After the first year of novelty—setting up his studio, joining the chess club, and volunteering with robotics teams—he began to feel a subtle but persistent sense that his projects "didn’t really matter" now that he was no longer contributing to a large R&D group. Over the next three years, he continued to attend community events and hiking club outings, but his wife noticed he talked more about his peak career achievements than about current plans, and he increasingly framed his days as "marking time" until the next trip or workshop rather than building toward anything. When he found himself repeatedly declining invitations to lead new STEM-art initiatives because he felt there was "no point" and started voicing worries that his best years were behind him, his primary care doctor, concerned by this change in outlook at an annual wellness visit, suggested a mental health evaluation.
narrative.chief_complaint: Lately I just feel like the future doesn’t hold much for me and that the meaningful part of my life is already over.
